title: Optimal Scheduling for the Big Long River

section_map.summary: The opening summary and abstract define the river-scheduling decision, compare four models, quantify the occupancy-crossover tradeoff, describe distribution distortion and robustness, and condition the final model choice on management preferences.

The introduction moves from river facts and the wildlife constraint through three optimization difficulties, then presents the naive, priority, density-perturbation, and bone-growth models as an explicit ladder of responses.
The notation section defines crossovers, trips, X, Y, T, P, two schedule-matrix orientations, open-campsite percentage, guaranteed travel distance, the multi-objective problem, and carrying capacity.

The assumptions collapse craft choice into trip length, forbid hybrid trips, set daily reach, borrow campsite spacing from two real rivers, remove launch-resource constraints, and discretize behavior to nightly campsite states.
The analysis explains why standard identical-machine scheduling and queueing abstractions do not directly fit an ordered sequence of unique river sections with nightly unit capacity.

The algorithm section first inserts whole trips into an empty schedule and diagnoses blocking and crossover failures, then changes to night-by-night priority scheduling with distance-per-day urgency and local crossover-aware campsite ranking.

The density model moves every active trip toward its equal-distance daily target in continuous mile space, sums signed local repulsion contributions, iterates until trips admit a one-to-one campsite mapping, and discards rare unresolved collisions.

The bone model replaces unrestricted crossovers with a deterministic greedy construction: alternate trip-length sequences, squeeze trajectories toward the center, insert the best feasible trip, saturate, and spread launch times.

The results compare Priority, Density Perturbation, Bones1, and Bones2 across campsite counts and target distributions using trips, open sites, crossovers, and distribution variance, then interpret scaling and initial-sequence effects.
The analysis checks five decision dimensions, traces short-trip skew and crossover growth, reports a failed removal experiment, and compares the temporal consistency of priority and bone schedules.

The strengths and weaknesses separate throughput, crossover, backtracking, distribution, departure-rate, sort probability, initial-bone, speed-limit, and launch-clustering effects for the two leading models.

The conclusion chooses Priority when occasional passing is acceptable, Bone Growth when zero crossover dominates, proposes time-window mixing, and identifies craft, campsite, speed, annealing, and initialization extensions.

The memo gives managers a two-algorithm choice, capacity and coverage ranges, schedule outputs, assumptions, and a possible mixed-model pricing strategy, while compressing or drifting from several body results.
Eight references provide river statistics, commercial itinerary context, scheduling and optimization books, and campsite-spacing data, but no code, seeds, raw schedules, or frozen experiment files.

assumptions.summary: Craft choice can be postponed because vessel type is strongly correlated with trip length and motor craft can cover trips that exceed oar reach.
Passengers do not switch boat type during a trip.
Motor craft can travel 64 miles per day and oar craft are later treated as capable of 32 miles per day under eight hours of travel.
Campsite spacing is modeled as uniform and tested at roughly five, 1.5, and one mile per campsite, giving Y=45, 150, and 225.
Launch labor, boats, docks, and daily release capacity are unlimited.
Only nightly campsite positions matter; within-day density and activities do not reduce travel distance.
Priority may be randomized through a sort probability p, while Density Perturbation treats all trips as equally important.
Bone feasibility can be screened by an alternating launch sequence and center-squeezed trajectories.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Problem constants supply a 225-mile river, 180-night scheduling horizon, six-to-eighteen campsite stops, and four- versus eight-mile-per-hour craft.
The cited 2007-2010 Grand Canyon counts list roughly 409-426 motor and 181-184 non-motor trips per year.
Campsite context cites 162 sites over 250 Colorado River miles and 185 sites over 180.6 Salmon River miles.
Figure 4 states 1978 trips in 180 days for 200 uniformly spaced campsites from mile 10 through mile 215.
The main table compares 19 rows across Priority, Density Perturbation, Bones1, and Bones2 with trips, open percentage, crossovers, and distribution variance.
At Y=225 uniform demand, Priority reports 2911 trips, 16.55 percent open, 28.93 crossovers per trip, and 1.30 in the ambiguous variance column.
At Y=225 uniform demand, Bones1 reports 1707 trips and 51.82 percent open; Bones2 reports 2107 trips and 46.80 percent open, both with zero crossovers.
Bones1 alternates mostly six and eighteen; Bones2 steps through shorter large-trip values and consequently favors shorter trips.
Eight references supply context and textbooks but no executable or frozen computational evidence.

models.summary: Represent the campsite occupied by trip i on night j, including launch and exit states.
Represent the trip hosted by campsite i on night j, with zero meaning empty.
Normalize the maximum scheduled trip count over 180 days by campsite count.
Rank trips by the average daily distance still required.
Create a signed local repulsion that grows as two proposed boat locations become closer.
Sum every neighboring boat's contribution before shifting boat j.
Weight shorter trip lengths more heavily in the triangle target distribution.
Maintain mutually interpretable trip-by-night and campsite-by-night schedule views.
Randomly select a remaining trip length and remove that length only after all launch nights fail.
Try equal daily progress, move to the nearest available campsite on conflicts, and accept only if every night is feasible.
Build the schedule one night at a time by adding departures, ordering active trips, and assigning their next campsites.
With probability p sort active trips by urgency; otherwise shuffle them to moderate systematic distribution skew.
Choose the campsite nearest current position plus remaining distance divided by remaining days.
When the best camp is occupied, restrict to reachable camps, remove occupied sites, rank crossover-free status before proximity, and choose the first.
Move finished trips to the completed schedule and carry unfinished trip-camp pairs into the next night.
Move each active trip to the mile position implied by equal remaining distance per remaining day.
Compute signed repulsion only for pairs within one campsite spacing, randomizing the sign for exact ties.
Sum contributions and subtract total density repeatedly until proposed locations are sufficiently separated.
Map separated positions one-to-one onto campsites and discard a trip in the rare unresolved collision case.
Alternate monotone increasing and decreasing trip-length sequences so a shorter trip does not finish before a longer trip ahead.
Pull trajectories toward the central trip to test the necessary packed configuration for a fixed launch-finish order.
Enumerate heuristic insertion points, score candidate trip types against the target distribution, and retain a feasible insertion.
Repeat best feasible insertion until no trip length can be added without a crossover.
Spread the saturated center-packed trajectories in time to make launches more uniform while retaining order.
Assign less flexible oar craft and more flexible motor craft within the bone construction, with spreading left incomplete.
Run campsite counts 45, 150, and 225 with uniform and triangle targets and compute the declared comparison metrics.
Grow and compare Bones1 and Bones2 to expose throughput and distribution sensitivity to the starting sequence.
Choose Priority for higher occupancy with passing, Bone Growth for zero crossovers, or mix them over time windows.

results_trace.summary: Density Perturbation reports 1978 trips in Figure 4 for Y=200, while the later table lists 1811 trips, 41.07 percent open, 19.07 crossovers, and 5.85 variance.
Priority increases from 546 trips at Y=45 uniform demand to 2911 at Y=225, while average crossovers rise from 4.37 to 28.93.
Priority open percentage falls from 23.80 at Y=45 uniform demand to 16.55 at Y=225, implying higher campsite occupancy.
Bones1 remains near 52 percent open and zero crossovers across the uniform scenarios, with roughly 7.5 trips per campsite.
Bones2 schedules more trips than Bones1 but has much larger distribution variance and roughly 9 trips per campsite.
For Y=225 triangle demand, Priority reports 2937 trips, 17.28 percent open, 29.06 crossovers, and 1.99 in the variance column.
Priority matches the target distribution better as campsite count increases, while Bone Growth increasingly saturates with shorter trips.
Removing the highest-crossover trips preferentially removes long trips and reduces campsite coverage by 10 to 15 percent.
Bone Growth produces temporally consistent no-crossover schedules using about half the campsites.
Priority is most useful when occupancy dominates and managers tolerate passing; useful sort probabilities were reported between 0.3 and 0.6.
Bone Growth guarantees zero crossover but depends strongly on starting bone, greedy scoring, and trajectory compression.
The paper recommends model mixing over different time windows when neither maximum occupancy nor zero crossover alone captures management preferences.

weaknesses.summary: Physical page 1 has no text layer; its Summary was visually transcribed and must not be treated as machine-extracted text coverage.

The abstract says Priority covers 80 percent and Bone Growth about 50 percent, while the memo compresses the range to 70 to 50 percent and the Y=225 table implies about 83.45 percent occupancy for Priority.
The abstract calls the solution nearly optimal without a global optimum, bound, or comparator against exact small instances.
The introduction says a failed naive trip is discarded, while the algorithm removes its trip length from the distribution after all launch nights fail; those are different rejection semantics.
The paper alternates among trip days, rafting days, nights, stops, six-to-eighteen, and seven-to-nineteen without one explicit indexing convention.
S1 uses campsite values through Y+1 while S2 uses campsite rows and trip identifiers through X, but the conversion, launch, exit, and zero conventions are not formalized.

Open Campsite percent is described as an unoccupied fraction but then said never to reach 100 percent for boundary reasons; the denominator and whether launch/exit cells count require a typed definition.
C(Y)=max X(Y)/Y depends on an unstated feasible-set maximum, target distribution, horizon, and crossover policy, so carrying capacity changes meaning across models.
Craft choice is postponed until after scheduling even though some short trips require daily distance beyond the assumed oar maximum.
The guaranteed-distance discussion derives 64 motor miles but later uses 32 oar miles without the same explicit derivation and ignores weather, flow, stops, and within-day congestion.
The campsite-spacing histogram lacks visible sample size, bin specification, source-cleaning procedure, uncertainty, and a direct mapping from the two source rivers to the synthetic river.
Unlimited launch equipment, labor, dock, and arrival capacity can create extreme daily clusters that the objective never penalizes.
Night-only discretization permits arbitrary within-day crossovers and congestion, then treats crossover penalties as a partial repair rather than testing travel feasibility.
The scheduling-theory comparison is qualitative and does not establish that integer programming or alternative network formulations are computationally infeasible.
The naive nearest-available rule does not define tolerance, tie-breaking probability, daily reach boundaries, or rollback after a later night fails.
Priority uses a probability-p sort-or-shuffle step, but no seed, repeated-run protocol, or uncertainty interval is supplied.
Ranking camps primarily by whether they incur a crossover is underspecified when multiple existing trips and order relations are present.
Priority removes trips that cannot be assigned on a night but does not backtrack to reuse space that those trips occupied on earlier nights.
The density model declares all trips equally important but still has to choose signs randomly at identical positions and choose which trip to discard in an unresolved collision.
Equation (1) is explicitly limited to nonzero separation within one campsite distance; exact ties are described by random mapping to plus or minus one outside the displayed formula.
Repeatedly subtracting density has no step size, stop tolerance, maximum iteration count, convergence proof, or test for oscillation and boundary violations.
A one-to-one campsite mapping is asserted for certain near-spacing patterns without a specified matching algorithm or proof for the full set of boats.
Figure 4 reports 1978 trips for Density Perturbation, while the main table reports 1811 for D.Pertb.; scenario or implementation differences are not reconciled.
Bone Heuristic 1 is presented as determining an optimal alternating sequence without proof that other no-crossover launch orders cannot dominate it.
Center squeezing is called a necessary condition but the travel-speed, campsite, launch, and finish constraints used in its feasibility test are not fully formalized.
The greedy score used to select the best inserted trip is not defined mathematically, and no tie rule or complexity analysis is given.
Bone Growth guarantees no crossovers for its constructed schedule but only claims a local optimum and is highly sensitive to the initial bone.
The motor-oar extension is incomplete because the spreading algorithm was not adjusted for the lower flexibility of oar craft.
The final table header is visually ambiguous as 'Var from Distr -10^4'; its scaling must be preserved as uncertain rather than silently read as multiplication or division.
The Density Perturbation row uses Y=200 while the other main comparisons use 45, 150, and 225, preventing a like-for-like ranking.
Bones2 produces more trips largely because it contains shorter trips and substantially misses the stated target distribution, so throughput and distribution fidelity cannot be merged.
Removing high-crossover trips reduced campsite coverage by 10 to 15 percent but no scenario, repeat count, or uncertainty is reported.
Priority crossover growth is described as exponential from three campsite settings without a fitted model, residuals, or broader scale sweep.
The conclusion converts roughly 29 crossovers per trip into less than one contact per hour without defining whether crossover count equals passenger contact or how trip duration enters.
The memo reports carrying capacity 12.5 to 7.5 and omits the approximately 9 trips-per-campsite Bones2 result stated in the body.
The memo says both algorithms can generate any desired trip ratio, while the results show persistent short-trip skew and especially poor Bones2 distribution matching.
